Build vs buy a gaming PC: compare the complete purchase cost

Compare the exact prebuilt with a complete DIY purchase plan. Include cooling, software, missing accessories and delivery; keep owned parts, checked offers and unknown prices separate.

By PC Part Performance · Published October 11, 2026 · Updated October 16, 2026

In this guide

  • Compare two systems that solve the same job
  • Make the purchase list complete before comparing totals
  • An incomplete subtotal is still incomplete
  • Separate observed cash costs from personal assumptions
  • Do not assume that Windows costs nothing
  • Value support and time explicitly
  • Use the result as a decision, not a slogan

Compare two systems that solve the same job

Begin with a workload and a display target, then write down two complete routes to that result. One route is the exact prebuilt configuration you can order. The other is a compatible DIY parts list. Matching only the CPU and graphics processor leaves room for large differences in memory, storage, cooling, networking or service. Decide which differences you accept and record them before comparing totals.

A complete DIY plan includes the motherboard, power supply, case and cooling as well as the most visible components. Add operating-system requirements, missing cables, wireless hardware and peripherals when your situation needs them. Components you already own can reduce the new cash outlay, but list them and check their condition and compatibility. Treating an unverified old part as a free solution can make a comparison look settled too early.

Intel

Make the purchase list complete before comparing totals

Mark every row as buy, already owned, included in another item, not needed or still unknown. “Included” requires the exact package description; “owned” requires a usable part and a compatibility check. Neither status means that a retailer quoted a zero price. Keep the prebuilt’s disclosed parts beside the DIY list so an unspecified PSU or cooler is a question to resolve rather than an assumed equivalent.

Cooling is an easy omission. The Ryzen 7 9800X3D boxed specification lists no included cooler, so a DIY quote for that CPU needs a separate cooling plan. The fact that a prebuilt names the same CPU does not tell you which cooler the system includes. Ask for the full configuration when cooling, networking or power-supply details could change your purchase.

A complete purchase checklist for your actual setup
RowWhat to recordWhen not to buy another
Core platformCPU, supported motherboard, correct memory and boot storageA verified compatible part is already owned
GraphicsExact card, or a deliberately supported integrated-graphics planYour existing graphics meet the intended job
CPU coolingExact cooler, mounting kit and any necessary separately supplied hardwareAn appropriate included or owned cooler is confirmed
Enclosure and powerCase, PSU and approved cables for that PSUCondition, fit and exact connectors are verified
Case airflowIncluded fans, additional needed fans and supported connectionsThe intended layout already has the required equipment
Networking and displayNeeded network connection, monitor and compatible display cableYour setup already provides them
Input and setupKeyboard, mouse, installation media and necessary toolsAvailable equipment is suitable
SoftwareChosen OS and licence or verified entitlementNo new purchase is needed under the actual terms
Order costsKnown delivery, applicable taxes and required service chargesA quoted amount explicitly includes the charge

AMD

An incomplete subtotal is still incomplete

A checked hardware subtotal is the sum of eligible observed prices, not the value of the whole computer. Keep missing new-item prices in a separate count. Keep manual quotes separate from observed offers, and distinguish sold-out listings from items you can currently order. An expired observation must not make an old sale look current.

When a required row is unresolved, compare complete scenarios rather than declaring the partial list cheaper. You can enter your own quote in the cost worksheet, clearly marked with its source and date, or wait for a supported offer. Retain a version of both lists so a substituted component or a later quote does not erase the basis of your earlier decision.

Separate observed cash costs from personal assumptions

Create one row for each cost and record its source. Keep a retailer-observed amount separate from your estimate of shipping or assembly time. Add tax consistently for both routes when it is known, and show it as unknown when it is not. Use the same region and currency. A converted foreign price is a planning assumption, not a domestic offer that you can buy on those terms.

For each exact new part or system, save the seller, condition, URL and observation time. A subtotal assembled from different days can be useful for planning, but it is not a guaranteed checkout total. Refresh stale rows together before making the purchase. Do not label the resulting difference as savings unless both routes remain available, comparable and complete when checked.

Use the same cost basis for both routes
CategoryDIY routePrebuilt route
HardwareEvery required new componentExact selected system configuration
SoftwareActual licence or verified existing entitlementIncluded edition and licence description
FulfilmentDelivery for all separate ordersSystem delivery and required extras
ServiceYour chosen repair and support planActual seller/manufacturer warranty terms
TimeA personal planning inputA personal planning input

Do not assume that Windows costs nothing

Record the operating-system edition and the licence basis for each route. An included prebuilt licence is part of that configuration; an existing licence on another machine may have conditions. Microsoft notes that a significant hardware change such as a motherboard replacement can require Windows reactivation. Matching the installed edition also matters. Those facts make software a checkable row rather than a casual zero.

Linking an account or retaining a product key does not, by itself, settle whether a licence can be transferred. Check the terms attached to your actual licence or ask the relevant provider. If that question remains open, leave the DIY software cost unresolved and compare a second scenario with a new licence. Avoid choosing a dubious key offer simply to make one route look cheaper.

Microsoft Support

Value support and time explicitly

A prebuilt can place more of the diagnosis and system repair behind one support route. A DIY build gives you control over the parts and assembly, but failures may involve different vendors. Neither description guarantees a pleasant repair. Read the actual terms and think about what happens if the machine stops working during an important week. Return shipping, backup equipment and your willingness to troubleshoot affect the decision.

If you assign money to your time, label it as your own assumption. Assembly, software setup, research and fault finding are separate activities, and beginners may value the learning itself. Run the comparison with and without a time allowance so that the cash difference stays visible. A personal hourly value is not a market measurement and should not be presented as a universal DIY labour charge.

Use the result as a decision, not a slogan

The cheaper complete route may be the right choice when it meets the job and you accept its service and component tradeoffs. A more expensive route can still make sense for a buyer who values exact part control or a particular support arrangement. State the reason and the remaining uncertainties beside the calculated difference. This is more informative than claiming that every prebuilt includes the same premium.

Save both configurations and the checked offer date. If a component substitution, unavailable item or expired offer changes one route, recalculate the comparison. The Build vs Buy tool is a worksheet for those inputs. It cannot supply missing prices, licence rights or a reliability result. A useful conclusion is conditional: under these verified costs and your stated preferences, one route suits you better.

  • Both routes meet the same workload and required features
  • Every required hardware and software row is present
  • Observed prices and personal assumptions are distinguishable
  • Currency, delivery and tax treatment are consistent
  • Support terms and unresolved licence questions are visible
